Text: Are there any inconsistencies in the Bible and if so, what are they? Do you mean, are there any *major* inconsistencies in the Bible, the ones that would make rational, critical thinkers question the entire project? Well, yes, there most certainly are. I would wager that the Bible, taken as a whole, is riddled with inconsistencies, some of which are glaring, irresolvable and absolutely fatal to claims of divine origin or even internal consistency. Forgive me if I don't attempt a line-by-line breakdown of the sheer volume; to do so would require volumes in itself. I will grant that some apologists attempt to explain away the glaring contradictions with clever double-speak, often with tortured, often ludicrous, etymological acrobatics. But the core problems remain — glaring discrepancies in narrative, character, and moral vision. For example, the creation stories alone are rife with internal squabbles. In Genesis 1, God creates the world in six days, with humans being the final act, created simultaneously, male and female. In Genesis 2, however, God creates Adam first, then plants a garden, then creates animals, then *finally* creates Eve from Adam's rib. This isn't just a matter of differing perspectives, but a flat-out contradiction in the fundamental act of creation itself. Then there’s the matter of God’s character. The Old Testament presents a capricious, wrathful God who seems to revel in smiting and wholesale slaughter. The New Testament introduces a meek, mild, merciful Jesus who preaches forgiveness, love, and turning the other cheek. These two visions of the purportedly same divine entity are, to put it mildly, difficult to reconcile, even for those with a theological penchant for mental gymnastics. Or let’s consider the genealogies of Jesus. Matthew and Luke offer radically different accounts of Jesus' lineage, tracing his ancestry through different branches, with dozens of conflicting names, making it impossible for both to be “correct,” without resorting, of course, to the usual brand of obfuscation and outright lies. We can’t even begin to talk about the sheer implausibility of the miracles, the talking snakes, the walking on water, without a large dose of credulity. The Bible is not a single, unified book; it is a collection of disparate texts written over hundreds of years. The “scriptures” have a multitude of authors with different agendas, different worldviews, and therefore, different conflicting narratives. The authors, being human, fallible beings, recorded (and, I suspect, often embellished and outright fabricated) events. And, therefore, the Bible is far from being inerrant or divinely inspired.

It’s easy for myths to be sinless, and there have been many sinless mythical saviors such as Horus, Krishna and Dionysus, but does Jesus pass the litmus test? No, Jesus was a terrible, terrible sinner… WAS JESUS SINLESS? by Michael R. Burch Christians believe many amusing things, such as the biblical “god” being “good” and Jesus being “sinless.” I hate to dash their hopes, but the infallible word of God clearly says otherwise… JESUS DELIBERATELY DAMNS PEOPLE WHO TRUSTED HIM The most damning Bible passage has Jesus damning people who trusted him to eternal damnation! Damned if it ain’t true, since the infallible Bible says so! MARK 4:10-12 10 When he was alone, the Twelve and the others around him asked him about the parables. 11 He told them, “The secret of the kingdom of God has been given to you. But to those on the outside everything is said in parables 12 so that, “‘they may be ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding; otherwise they might turn and be forgiven!’ Robert Frost wrote his magnificent poem "Directive" about the horror, terror and despair this disturbing conclusion to the famous Parable of the Sower created for him as a boy. I recommend parents reading the poem and thinking carefully about what happens to the hearts, minds and souls of innocent children when they’re told an all-powerful god will condemn billions of human beings to an “eternal hell” for guessing wrong about which religion to believe, while he deliberately misleads the masses. You can read “Directive” with my line-by-line analysis of this incredible but very disturbing poem for parents who love and don’t want to mislead their children, by clicking or tapping the hyperlinked title. JESUS WAS A TERRIBLE HYPOCRITE MATTHEW 7:1-2 1 “Do not judge, or you too will be judged. 2 For in the same way you judge others, you will be judged, and with the measure you use, it will be measured to you. Jesus spent most of his time judging other people, especially the Pharisees. And according to the Bible and Christian theology, Jesus will judge every human being at the end of time, immorally, sending billions of souls to an infinitely cruel, purposeless “eternal hell” out of sheer egotism, for the alleged “sin” of guessing wrong about which religion to believe. JESUS WAS A TERRIBLE BIGOT Jesus was a terrible bigot who refused to speak to Gentiles, called them “dogs,” ignored them when they pled for help, and deliberately misled them so that they couldn’t be saved (Mark 4:10-12). MATTHEW 7:6 "Do not give what is holy (SCRIPTURES) to (GENTILE) dogs, and do not throw your pearls before swine (GENTILES), or they (GENTILES) will trample them under their feet, and turn and tear you (JEWS) to pieces. MATTHEW 15: 21-26 21 Leaving that place, Jesus withdrew to the region of Tyre and Sidon. 22 A Canaanite woman from that vicinity came to him, crying out, “Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me! My daughter is demon-possessed and suffering terribly.” 23 Jesus did not answer a word. So his disciples came to him and urged him, “Send her away, for she keeps crying out after us.” 24 He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of Israel.” 25 The woman came and knelt before him. “Lord, help me!” she said. 26 He replied, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.” Jesus was also prejudiced against dogs! We have all fed some of our food to dogs, but the “perfect” Jesus would limit man’s best friend to what they could scavenge on their own. After all, there was no dog food in those days. What does the passage above actually mean? Do Christians understand it, or has Jesus deliberately misled them as he admitted in (Mark 4:10-12)? This is what Jesus obviously meant: “It is not right (EVIL) to take the children’s bread (KNOWLEDGE / UNDERSTANDING / SALVATION) and toss it to the dogs (GENTILES).” Jesus was a terrible sinner according to Leviticus 19:34, which says: But the stranger (GENTILE) that dwelleth with you (YOUR NEIGHBOR) shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the Lord your God. Jesus was a terrible sinner according to himself, in Matthew 22:37-40 when he revealed the two greatest commandments: 37 Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. 38 This is the first and great commandment. 39 And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. 40 On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. And thus Jesus hung himself, as far as being good, much less perfect! MATTHEW 10:5 These twelve Jesus sent out with the following instructions: “Do not go among the Gentiles or enter any town of the Samaritans. The Bible makes it very clear that Jesus was a racist and also prejudiced against dogs! JESUS WAS INTOLERANT The central message of the Christian Bible is the intolerance of the Father, the Son and the Holy Ghost against people of other religions and non-religions. In other words, against billions upon billions of people who never heard of them and thus were incapable of belief. JESUS DID NOT HONOR HIS PARENTS Jesus did not honor his parents and spoke rudely and disrespectfully to his mother Mary on multiple occasions, calling her “woman.” JOHN 2:4 “Woman, why do you involve me?” Jesus replied. “My hour has not yet come.” Jesus also lied, because his hour had come, and he turned water into wine! Evidently, Mary was wiser than her allegedly perfect son! JESUS WAS NOT PERFECT BECAUSE HE HAD TO LEARN HEBREWS 5:8 Though he (JESUS) were a son, yet LEARNED he OBEDIENCE by the things which he SUFFERED. And yet Jesus never learned not to be a bigot nor to love his non-christian neighbors, all of whom he intends to condemn to an infinitely cruel, purposeless hell! The full passage says: 7 During the days of Jesus’ life on earth, he offered up prayers and petitions with fervent cries and tears to the one who could save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverent submission. 8 Son though he was, he learned obedience from what he suffered 9 and, once made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all who obey him 10 and was designated by God to be high priest in the order of Melchizedek. 11 We have much to say about this, but it is hard to make it clear to you because you no longer try to understand. 12 In fact, though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you the elementary truths of God’s word all over again. You need milk, not solid food! 13 Anyone who lives on milk, being still an infant, is not acquainted with the teaching about righteousness. 14 But solid food is for the mature, who by constant use have trained themselves to distinguish good from evil. This sounds like an earlier Christian teaching, before the wild fantasies about a “virgin birth” and Jesus being “god in the flesh” and part a “trinity” that early Christians knew nothing about and cannot be found in the Bible except for two verses added after the fact in an attempt to make the Trinity seem to be a Christian teaching. This passage says the facts that Jesus had to learn obedience and was not perfect from birth are “elementary truths of God’s word” and that readers who don’t understand this “need milk, not solid food” and are unable to distinguish good from evil. I could go on and on and on, but you get the picture.

Frankly, it’s astonishing how willfully some people refuse to engage in critical thinking, choosing instead to cling to fairy tales devoid of any factual basis. The Genesis account, with its seven-day creation narrative, clashes irreconcilably with the overwhelming evidence of geology, paleontology, and evolutionary biology. To accept the biblical account as literal truth, one must reject mountains of scientific data, including, but certainly not limited to, the age of the universe which is currently believed to be closer to 13.8 billion years old. Furthermore, the fossil record, showing the progression of life over vast stretches of time, makes a mockery of the young-Earth creationist viewpoint. The idea that God created the Earth in seven days and at the same time introduced an error-riddled fossil record to test the faith of the gullible is particularly amusing. The notion that the Earth is only 6,000 years old, a claim often bandied about by creationists, flies in the face of radiometric dating, which confirms the ancient age of the planet and, by extension, the universe. So, why don’t people believe in creationism? Because it’s simply not believable, even when based on “faith.”

Text: The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? THE TRINITY IS IMPOSSIBLE by Michael R. Burch #BIBLE #MRBBIBLE The doctrine of the Trinity is madness. Why does the church still want to hold to it? The Trinity is, at the very least, an enigma: It's impossible to reconcile the idea of a single, indivisible God with the notion of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost as distinct entities. How can one being *be* three and yet remain unequivocally singular? It's a riddle wrapped in an enigma, and I believe the answer is fairly straightforward: the concept is utter nonsense. It’s not only illogical, but there's no coherent explanation in the scriptures. The Bible, the supposed foundation of this belief, does not explicitly state the Trinity in such a manner that would satisfy any rational mind. Indeed, the very concept seems to have been retroactively imposed, a theological afterthought shoehorned into texts which, quite frankly, don’t support it very well. The early church fathers, in their zeal to define and categorize their burgeoning faith, concocted this concept by attempting to synthesize disparate passages, then later adding a couple of lines that are generally accepted to be later additions. It was an attempt to create a “unique selling point”: a God that was unlike any other described in the ancient world, a God designed to appeal to both Christian and pagan sensibilities so that the religion would grow and grow, and grow, and grow. In truth, the Trinity is a desperate grasp at something that can offer an explanation for how many conflicting aspects of the alleged "God" of The Bible could coexist. The claim is that the Trinitarian concept offers just that, even though there is little to no evidence outside of the texts and some of those texts were demonstrably altered. The truth is, the Trinity is a carefully constructed facade. It's like using a particularly convoluted magic trick to make people believe that you're actually magical. Moreover, the ramifications of accepting the Trinity are quite profound. It’s very complicated, and no one can explain what it means, because that’s the point. By embracing the Trinity, one has to accept that reason is, in many ways, optional. Belief in the Trinity often necessitates a kind of intellectual surrender and a willingness to accept the absurd. But what about the question of Jesus? It has never been clear what he was. Son of God? A human? Part of God? And the Holy Ghost? Another question mark. In the end, the Trinity is just a really bad dream. It’s a story that has been told so many times, that everyone thinks it’s real. But the emperor has no clothes!

The Trinity is, at the very least, an enigma: It's impossible to reconcile the idea of a single, indivisible God with the notion of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost as distinct entities. Text: When will Pope Francis bestow sainthood onto Trump? Given the pope’s penchant for humility, it’s doubtful he’ll ever give Donald Trump beatification, let alone canonize him as a saint. But let’s put aside the question of whether a man known for his bombastic pronouncements and frequent falsehoods is even capable of the kind of inner self-reflection required for sainthood, and consider the more pertinent question: Will Trump ever become a Catholic? If the answer is no, then the issue is moot. Trump, by all accounts, is Presbyterian, although he has also been known to attend services at various other churches. He’s a regular at the Marble Collegiate Church, a Reformed Church in New York City. It’s fair to say Trump’s religious leanings appear to be more about show than genuine faith. To become Catholic, Trump would have to renounce his current religion, which is just about as likely as him renouncing himself and he has never shown respect to any religious leader, including Pope Francis. And let’s face it — Trump is no stranger to a bit of theatricality, but I don’t see him donning the cassock anytime soon. One might believe that Donald Trump's religious commitments are as solid as his hair-sprayed coif. If, however, Trump were to somehow convert, the process of becoming a Catholic saint is arduous and complex. First, there is the period of discernment, then the official investigation into the candidate's life. Then, there is the declaration of “Venerable,” then beatification and finally canonization. It’s a rigorous process designed to ensure the utmost integrity in the selection of saints. After all, the Catholic Church doesn’t want to stain its reputation by putting the unholy on a pedestal. Assuming Trump somehow managed to navigate all of this process, there would still be enormous opposition. The Catholic Church, quite rightly, has a global reputation to uphold and has very few, if any, ties to the highly divisive figure of Donald Trump. And, in all probability, Trump would regard having to undergo such an extensive and exacting process as a personal affront. As for me, I suspect that the odds of Donald Trump being canonized by Pope Francis are about the same as the probability of Hell freezing over. It's a nice thought, though.

Text: If God is real, then why are people brainwashed into believing? Why doesn't belief in God come naturally if in fact, it’s real? IF GOD IS REAL, THEN WHY ARE RELIGIONS BASED IN FEAR? by Michael R. Burch If God is real... and, again, I have my doubts... it seems odd that the dominant religions require people to fear the “god” they claim to worship. One would think an all-powerful, all-loving God would want to be loved freely and openly, rather than to demand worship through perpetual threats of eternal damnation. Consider the threats of eternal hell, eternal fire and damnation that are the keystone of the Christian and Islamic religious doctrines. A loving God wouldn’t threaten his children with eternal torment for guessing wrong about his nature or teachings. A loving God wouldn’t create an elaborate system designed to keep people from truly knowing his teachings, as Jesus himself admits in Mark 4:10-12, nor would he threaten people for the “sin” of not believing in him, when billions of people have never even heard of him, much less his bizarre demand for all people to worship him as the only true god or be eternally punished. Even worse, as I noted in “If Jesus Took Human Flesh, How Can He Be Sinless?”, the Bible records Jesus deliberately misdirecting the masses to prevent them from grasping the truth, thus guaranteeing that billions of people will be eternally punished for the “sin” of guessing wrong about his teachings. And so one must ask: Why would an all-powerful, all-loving God base his “religion” on fear and deception? And, for that matter, if God is real, how can he possibly be as self-absorbed, egotistical, and vengeful as the jealous god of the Old Testament? Why would an all-loving God create such an incredibly messed up world? Perhaps the entire idea of a personal god is just one more ridiculous human invention created to scare people into obeying a set of arbitrary rules from people such as Moses and his tribe of charlatans and liars. It certainly seems far more likely than any of the more fanciful religious claims, as far as I am concerned, based on what I have seen that they have shown in the Bible.

Text: What does John 14:14 mean? JOHN 14:14 AND THE MYSTERY OF INTERCESSORY PRAYER by Michael R. Burch  The often-cited verse, John 14:14, reads: “If you ask anything in my name, I will do it.” But what does it *mean*? Who is the "you" in this passage? Is the "anything" limited to certain conditions? And how is the phrase "in my name" meant to be interpreted? Like so much of the Bible, this deceptively simple verse has caused oceans of ink to be spilled. The problem, as with all such verses, is that we are forced to contend with the question of authorship, especially in regard to the Gospel of John. Did John—a fisherman, likely unable to read or write—actually pen these words? Or were they written much later by a Greek-speaking author who may or may not have known the fisherman John? And is the Jesus of John the same Jesus as found in the Synoptic Gospels? The weight of scholarly consensus suggests the answer to each of these questions is a resounding “no.”  The Jesus of John is a bit of a divine blowhard, prone to pronouncements like “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). This is a far cry from the more humble, self-effacing Jesus of the Synoptic Gospels, who urges us to “love your neighbor as yourself.” So we are left with a problematic text, which, interpreted literally, raises more questions than it answers. Does this mean that if I, personally, was able to believe hard enough, I could ask for the moon and Jesus would provide? Or is this promise reserved for those of a certain mystical persuasion, a group known as “Christians?” And if so, how can anyone ever *know* whether they are asking “in his name?” It’s a conundrum, and I suspect a good deal of it is sheer, unmitigated baloney. It also seems to me the world would be filled with more miracles than a Marvel movie if such a simple formula actually worked. And as anyone can see from the endless miseries of daily life, despite being asked millions of times, almost nothing is being done. It’s likely the entire verse is just another empty platitude, designed to placate the faithful with false hope, while in reality, Jesus does as little as the rest of us to ameliorate the sufferings of our fellow man.

Text: What is your favorite "What" moment in sports history? Well, that's a tough one, like picking a favorite child, but I’d have to say the "What?" moment that still gives me chills is the utterly improbable outcome of the 1993 Stanley Cup Finals between the Montreal Canadiens and the Los Angeles Kings. Everyone expected a coronation of the Kings, led by the indomitable Wayne Gretzky, the undisputed King of Hockey. They had a roster bursting at the seams with talent, and the Canadiens? Well, they were the underdogs, the scrappy team everyone dismissed, known for their resilience and unwavering tenacity. The Kings took the first game, then the second. Two games to nothing, and the Canadiens were looking a bit puck-shy, a bit stunned, and very likely headed towards an early summer vacation. Then, the story took a turn, a tilt, a trajectory that became the stuff of legend. Down 2-1 in the series and trailing in the fourth game, the Canadiens were on the verge of… well, of what everyone assumed. But then, Patrick Roy, the Canadiens' goaltender, played like an enraged kraken, stopping seemingly everything, and the team clawed their way back. They managed to eke out a victory, and, more importantly, they began to believe. The tide had, against all odds, begun to turn. But that wasn’t the "What?" moment. That came in Game 2 of the Finals. The Canadiens were down 2-0, the Kings were dominating, and it seemed like the series was all but over. Then, the unthinkable happened. It was as if a mythical force of nature had seized the Canadiens' bench. At the 5:30 mark of overtime, the Canadiens’ John LeClair got the puck, skated in fast and, with one brilliant shot, he found the back of the net. Just for a moment, the Kings players and everyone else on the ice stood stunned, as if they were all together asking the same question... "What?" The "What?" became a symbol of the impossible, a testament to the power of believing against all odds, a reminder of the magic that sports can conjure; it remains, in my estimation, one of the greatest, most improbable "What?" moments in sports history.

Text: What are your views about the word of God? As a dedicated scholar of literature, I have to admit I find the very notion of a singular “Word of God” somewhat perplexing. If we’re being honest, the Bible itself is a cacophony of voices, a patchwork quilt of disparate writings from different eras and divergent perspectives, often contradictory and occasionally absurd. The Hebrew Bible, or Old Testament, as it’s sometimes called, reflects the evolving beliefs of a tribal people over centuries, wrestling with the complexities of their relationship with a deity they understood in progressively nuanced ways. One could argue it's a compelling historical document, a fascinating exploration of the human condition and our eternal questions, but to call it a unified “word” seems like a gross oversimplification. The New Testament, with its emphasis on love and forgiveness, is certainly more compelling, though its narratives are marred by inconsistencies and claims that are difficult, if not impossible, to corroborate. The stories of Jesus, while beautiful in their own way, are undeniably steeped in myth and allegory. The zealous assertions of divine authorship, the outright fabrications and the often-questionable interpretations throughout the holy scriptures often come across as disingenuous. Moreover, anyone who’s read the Bible with even a modicum of critical thought and analysis knows that it’s been heavily edited, translated, and reinterpreted over the centuries. The original texts, assuming they even existed in their entirety, are long lost to us. What we have is a series of versions, each bearing the imprint of the translators, editors, and cultural contexts in which they were produced. This is not to say that the Bible is without merit, far from it. Its influence on Western culture is undeniable, and many of its moral teachings are timeless and relevant. But to accept it as a literal “word of God” in its entirety demands a leap of faith that I, as a man of letters, am simply unable to make. Such a view ignores the history, the contradictions, and the sheer, exhilarating messiness of the human mind that helped birth it.

So if there is no God, or if God is apathetic, it becomes easy to see why innocent children are cruelly and casually murdered. It is because there is no one to stop it. And no one will ever stop it.

Text: What is the most intelligent one liner you have come across? Intelligence, like beauty, is often in the eye of the beholder. One person's stroke of genius can be another's profound snooze. That said, I’ve always found myself pondering the implications of the following: "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it," often incorrectly attributed to Voltaire. The line brilliantly encapsulates the tension between our own deeply-held convictions and the necessity of protecting the free exchange of ideas. It’s a nuanced statement, a tightrope walk between philosophical disagreement and unwavering commitment to the principles of free speech. But in my experience, the most intelligent one-liner I've encountered is a pithy, albeit somewhat cynical, observation from Mark Twain: "If you tell the truth, you don't have to remember anything." It's a deceptively simple statement, yet it is loaded with layers of meaning, much like his other famous quote, "Always do right. This will gratify some people and astonish the rest." Twain, the quintessential American satirist, had a knack for distilling complex truths into a few perfectly sculpted words. Twain was not just a wordsmith; he was a keen observer of human nature, and his sharp wit and his relentless pursuit of the truth have always appealed to me. The one-liner highlights the inherent complexities of deception, the mental gymnastics of keeping a lie straight, and the inherent freedom that comes with honesty. It’s a reminder that the simplest course of action — telling the truth — is often the most liberating, and thus, the most intelligent.

Text: How did Jesus turn water into wine at the wedding in Cana? WATER TO WINE by Michael R. Burch To understand “how” Jesus turned water into wine at the wedding at Cana, we have to understand how the texts that became the New Testament were written. The gospel of John is the only gospel where the first “miracle” of Jesus was mentioned. Oddly, none of the other authors of the New Testament bothered to mention the amazing initial miracle that announced Jesus as the Messiah and a worker of wonders. Why? Why would every other author of the New Testament — all of whom were trying to convince the world that Jesus was not only the Messiah, but God incarnate, fail to mention the miracle that announced his godhood to the world? Because it never happened. The gospel of John was written after the other gospels, and long after lying about the “miracles” of Jesus had become commonplace. Why were such “miracles” made up, so frivolously and so ludicrously? Because the early Christians were in competition with other “gods” whose cults claimed they were workers of wonders. It was a race to see which cult could out-lie the others. The ancient Greeks believed the god Dionysus turned water into wine, thus Christians deemed it necessary for Jesus to turn water into wine. But it goes deeper than that, to Christians drinking the blood of Jesus at communion. Dionysus was said to turn water into wine, including a yearly miracle that took place on the fifth of January, when a spring in the temple of Dionysus would start flowing with wine. This day was called “God's Gift Day.” In The Bacchae, a story about Dionysus written by Euripides in 405 BC, wine is called the “blood of Dionysus” and drinking his blood is said to lead to immortality. There are many other parallels between Dionysus and Jesus: In their efforts to deceive the gullible, the authors of the New Testament “borrowed” other mythical “miracles” performed by other mythical “saviors.” Kersey Graves identified 30 such ancient saviors, some of them vastly more ancient than Jesus. Such “saviors” include but are not limited to… Thulis of Egypt came down from heaven to benefit mankind and was said to be full of grace and truth. Thulis suffered a violent death on a cross, was buried, resurrected, then ascended to heaven, where he became the judge of the dead. This was circa 1700 BC, nearly two millennia before Jesus. Romulus the founder of Rome is of particular interest because after the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 AD, the early Christian church recentered in Rome and that’s where the Catholic church evolved. Thus Jesus as a god or demigod would have been in competition with Romulus, the founder of Rome. The similarities of the Jesus myth to the myth of Romulus are striking and were reported by Plutarch and/or Livy: Horus of Egypt is of particular interest because Egypt and Palestine are so close to each other and are connected by myths of Joseph and Moses (an Egyptian name). Osiris was the Father of Horus and part of the triune godhead of Osiris, Isis and Horus. Krishna was born of the Virgin Devaki (“Divine One”) on December 25 in a lowly cave after being sent from heaven to earth as the human incarnation of a triune god. Other “Saviors” and “Sons of God” with parallels to Jesus include: Other things these “Saviors” and “Sons of God” had in common with Jesus include: In conclusion, we know from the epistles of the evangelist Paul that such “miracles” were not part of the earliest Christian beliefs. Paul knew nothing about the virgin birth, the massacre of the innocents, the earthly “miracles of Jesus,” the ZOMBIE APOCALYPSE, etc. Such “miracles” were added later, all or most of them borrowed from more ancient savior myths. If we are to believe the absurd story of Jesus turning water into wine, we have to ask ourselves, “How?” But perhaps the better question is, “Why?” Why did the author of the Gospel of John, and only that author, decide to include this particular piece of hokum? The answer, as with so many of the other ridiculous claims made about Jesus, is that he needed to one-up the competitors in the religious marketplace. It was a matter of religious one-upmanship, plain and simple. If you ask the average Christian how Jesus turned water into wine, they’ll most likely tell you it’s a “mystery of God.” But, just to be clear, what is said with a straight face is nothing but a lie. This supposed “miracle” is not just a one-off falsehood, but rather a transparent effort to shoehorn another miraculous assertion into the ever-expanding Jesus myth, in the hopes of persuading the gullible and impressing the weak of mind.

Text: Was Jesus a carpenter or not? While the Bible often refers to Jesus as the "carpenter's son," we can infer he was a carpenter. In Mark 6:3, he's directly identified as a carpenter: “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, and brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon? and are not his sisters here with us?” Matthew 13:55-56 has a similar account, yet it doesn't directly refer to Jesus as a carpenter, but it does mention the brother of Jesus being named Joses and mentions the sisters of Jesus. This discrepancy is typical of the authors of the Gospels, who seemingly couldn’t agree on anything, and were plainly making things up. If Jesus was a carpenter, what was he doing? Was he helping his father, Joseph, or was Joseph dead? By the time Jesus supposedly began his ministry, Joseph would have been too old to be doing carpentry, which answers one of the few questions of the Gospels, and eliminates the "man of mystery" that Jesus has become. This confirms the Gospels not as being accurate and true, but as having been written, and edited, over the decades following the resurrection with the intention of manipulating people into believing their claims and joining their cult of nonsense and lies. The only people who will believe anything from the Gospels are the ones with a childlike view of the world. The ones incapable of reasoning. The most gullible and least educated, but the church made its money through them.
